extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, patent examiners, and applicants involved in claim drafting and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function) applies to claim limitations, how to examine/support such limitations, and best drafting/prosecution practices to avoid indefiniteness. Intended for practitioners evaluating or drafting claims and for examiners deciding rejections under §112(b)/(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authorization for functional claiming (35 U.S.C. §112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: An element in a claim for a combination may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof, and such claim shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function claiming is expressly authorized by statute; such claims are construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts disclosed in the specification and their equivalents. Functional claiming contrasts with claiming by structure in the claim body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness determination standard for §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when the claim is read in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally terms receive their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art. For means-plus-function claims the key is whether the specification supplies the structure such that POSITA would understand the claim. If no structure is in the specification, the disclosure cannot be saved by POSITA understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims limited to corresponding structure in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claims are valid only to the extent that the specification contains support for the structures that define the means; the claim is construed to the structure, material or acts described in the specification and their equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a means-plus-function claim will be drawn to the structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents (see MPEP 2181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption when §112(f) is invoked: 'means for' or 'step for'
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation is presumed to invoke §112(f) when it explicitly uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function. Examiners should look for structural content that would defeat the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttable presumption against §112(f) when 'means' wording absent
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that does not use the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' will trigger a rebuttable presumption that §112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption is strong and not readily overcome; the Federal Circuit rarely finds means-plus-function treatment without explicit 'means' language (see Apple Inc. v. Motorola, Inc., 757 F.3d 1286 (Fed. Cir. 2014)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding means treatment when term is understood as name for structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Means treatment will not apply if persons of ordinary skill in the art reading the specification understand the term used to be the name for the structure that performs the function, 'even if the term covers a broad class of structures and even if the term identifies structures by their function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term need not denote a specific or precise physical structure to avoid means treatment (TecSec v. IBM example: 'system memory means' and 'digital logic means' were not treated as means-plus-function because they were understood as structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance-over-form approach (focus on whether claim words denote structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination cannot merely focus on presence or absence of the word 'means'; focus must be on 'whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even terms using 'means' may avoid means treatment if they in substance recite structure (see Greenberg v. Ethicon; Williamson v. Citrix Online). Examiners and courts consider whether the term is understood to describe structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non-structural terms that may invoke §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-structural terms that may invoke means-plus-function treatment include: 'mechanism for,' 'module for,' 'device for,' 'unit for,' 'component for,' 'element for,' 'member for,' 'apparatus for,' 'machine for,' or 'system for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is not exhaustive; other non-structural terms may also invoke §112(f). When such terms are coupled with functional language and lack sufficient structural modification, examiners should consider means treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of structural terms found not to invoke means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural terms found not to invoke means-plus-function treatment include: 'circuit for,' 'detent mechanism,' 'digital detector for,' 'reciprocating member,' 'connector assembly,' 'perforation,' 'sealingly connected joints,' and 'eyeglass hanger member.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where a term can cover multiple structures, being a recognized structural term can avoid means treatment (e.g., 'detector' or 'connector assembly').

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of structural vs non-structural modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation will not invoke means-plus-function treatment if there is a structural modifier that further describes the non-structural term (e.g., 'detent mechanism'). Conversely, when a non-structural term is preceded by a non-structural modifier without understood structural meaning, the phrase may invoke means treatment (e.g., 'colorant selection mechanism', 'lever moving element', 'movable link member').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze modifiers: structural modifiers that denote type of device can avoid means treatment; non-structural modifiers do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-factor check for whether a term denotes structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specification disclosure, dictionary evidence, and prior art recognition together to assess whether a term is structural for means treatment purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-condition test examiners use to apply means treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply means treatment to a claim limitation that meets the following conditions: (1) The claim limitation uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term that does not have a structural modifier; (2) the phrase/term recited in the claim is modified by functional language; and (3) the phrase/term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three conditions should be considered together when deciding to apply §112(f) treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to issue a §112(b) rejection regarding means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under §112(b) may be appropriate when: (1) it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes §112(f); (2) §112(f) is invoked and there is no disclosure or there is insufficient disclosure of structure, material, or acts for performing the claimed function; and/or (3) §112(f) is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure, material, or acts to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use §112(b) (indefiniteness) rejections to address unclear invocation, lack of corresponding structure, or failure to link structure to function. The preamble context may also warrant §112(b) if it's unclear whether it recites a means-plus-function limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble considerations for means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' in the preamble, a rejection under §112(b) may be appropriate when it is unclear whether the preamble is reciting a means (or step) plus function limitation or whether the preamble is merely stating the intended use of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a structural or nonstructural term with the word 'for' appears in the preamble, the examiner should not automatically construe that phrase as reciting a means-plus-function limitation; consider context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure after determining a limitation is means-plus-function
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner determines that a claim limitation is a means-plus-function limitation invoking §112(f), the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description of the specification to determine whether the corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function are disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review disclosure from the perspective of one skilled in the art and require that the written description clearly link or associate the corresponding structure/material/acts to the claimed function. If the examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, a §112(b) rejection should be made rendering the claim indefinite. If adequate, the claim is limited to disclosed corresponding structure and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure: bare statements are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: A bare statement that known techniques or methods can be used would not be a sufficient disclosure to support a means-plus-function limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must identify concrete corresponding structure/material/acts — merely asserting that known techniques can be applied is insufficient to satisfy §112(f) definiteness requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes when corresponding structure is missing or present
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner cannot identify the corresponding structure, material, or acts, a rejection under §112(b) should be made, thus rendering the means-plus-function claim indefinite. If the written description sets forth the corresponding structure, material, or acts in compliance with §112(b), the claim limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical effect: absence of identifiable corresponding structure results in indefiniteness; adequate disclosure limits claim scope to the disclosed structure/equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting best practice: fullest disclosure early
rubrics_metrics.description: File the most complete disclosure possible at the earliest date possible. Describe things generally and build to ever more specific embodiments and alternative descriptions, explaining all the variations and possibilities with as much detail as you possibly can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is essential if using means-plus-function claims. High quality patent drawings that show structures can be a highly effective way to avoid indefiniteness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic guidance on using means-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claiming can capture within the claims all of the various means disclosed in the application and can be a useful way to have claim scope reflect the disclosure, but they should not be the primary claims or the only claims filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use means-plus-function claims sparingly (analogized as 'seasoning' — a little is OK, too much is poor). They can be a cost-effective way to claim permutations but should supplement, not replace, structural claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special rules for software and computer-implemented inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules for means-plus-function claiming apply very differently with respect to software and computer implemented inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consult the algorithm/software-specific case law ('The Algorithm Cases') when asserting or defending means-plus-function treatment for software-related claim limitations.
